### The default run takes 4.6 minutes where it took 16: Rust's test binaries and the Python files run several at a time, and a passed run covers what it left unread

change `lptpzxuplxky` · [log `c8ab0ad3ad4d`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/853b40ba-32fd-4638-8789-b2c3159d775a/c8ab0ad3ad4d33d4d4223a430c2d96f247b6a642eebcba02d4137eaac45e5298.jsonl.gz)

test_costs.py run: cargo only builds the Rust test binaries (--no-run), and they then run several at a time (--rust-jobs, by default half the CPUs, at most 4, and one per 1.5 GB of a job's memory limit), the longest first by what each took the last time (kept in the target directory). The Python test files run several at a time too (--python-jobs, 3 by default, 2 in a job); a file that fails has its second run alone after the others, so two files that disturbed each other show as flaky. The proof tier still runs one binary at a time, and --rust-jobs 1 --python-jobs 1 is the run as it was. Measured on this machine: the Rust binaries 707 s one after another in the first job, 403 s three at a time under a six-CPU limit beside another test job (peak 3.4 GB), 230 s four at a time; the whole default run 276 s, 49 of 49 passed, nothing flaky.

Three Rust test files prepare their fixtures together and not one after another, with the same assertions: observations.rs's Box Office examples test builds its ten patched examples four at a time (the binary went from 146 s to 71 s alone) and keeps the Gradle build between runs under a hash of its sources, tasks and JDK; application_core.rs and application_core_joint.rs compile their nineteen fixture builds four at a time.

default_tests.py: a run in the pipeline's fresh export records which files nothing opened and which folders nothing listed, from their access times (one packed line in its log; 'default_tests.py unread JOB' lists it), and a passed run then covers a later commit that only modifies those files or adds and removes files inside those folders. lib/ always counts as read, a rename is never covered, and a filesystem without access times records nothing. A probe of the Python half in an export left 546 entries unread, among them the example pages, CLAUDE.md and the runtime page. 'default_tests.py flaky' counts flaky tests over the collected runs. sync.py adopt-logs takes a log as a hard link where it can. Verified by the default run above, which includes the new tests of each piece (stand-in cargo and made-up runs); the inventory has the eight new Python rows, added by hand as the handoff note says.

### /run-brief: a watcher runs a feature brief on command, with a foundation stage on Fable 5.2 before its streams

change `xppmwwppknky` · [log `c8ab0ad3ad4d`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/853b40ba-32fd-4638-8789-b2c3159d775a/c8ab0ad3ad4d33d4d4223a430c2d96f247b6a642eebcba02d4137eaac45e5298.jsonl.gz)

A brief of llm-dlc/loops/ was started by hand, and its run was known to run-streams.sh only through a list of five names in the script. A local skill, /run-brief (.claude/skills/run-brief, not part of the plugin), now runs any brief with a watcher session on Opus 5.5, as /prove-java-change runs a proof. Its tool is llm-dlc/tools/brief_run.py: a preflight that finds what run-streams.sh would stop at before anything starts and says what the verification runner may keep beside this many loops (budget --apply lowers verification/pipeline.local.toml for the run); a foundation stage, one Fable 5.2 session at high effort given the user's instruction to start the work itself, build the foundation it sees fit and update the brief for the agents that take over, in a workspace of its own so no other session's uncommitted files meet its commits; land, which brings its commits to the default line, moved forward or by a merge with the generated trace files regenerated, and takes back a merge that conflicts in real work; start, which runs run-streams.sh detached; and wait, which returns only what needs the watcher (a blocked loop, a failing integration check, an open decision, a missing verification loop, a summary every 30 minutes, the end).

run-streams.sh takes a brief by name or file and reads its streams from the brief's Loop settings (- streams: a, b); the five older briefs keep their lists, a brief with no streams runs as its own loop, --plan prints what was read, and a stream brief's fork is optional. With a watcher, a loop that ends blocked is put to it (conductor.py's new blocked question: rerun or leave, half an hour at most), so a decision reaches its stream during the run instead of after it; the verdict is a decision in the record. A stream waiting on jobs is checked every minute, not every five. The brief template gains the streams setting, how a brief is run, and an opt-in test policy (tests: queued: the default run as a job per commit instead of a wait before each next piece), which CLAUDE.md names as an exception for such a brief's own loops.

Verified by llm-dlc/tools/test_brief_run.py (24 tests on a made-up jj repository with stand-ins for claude, feature-loop.sh and sync.py, including run-streams.sh end to end: a blocked stream run again at the watcher's word, one left without an answer, a brief with no streams, and a run started and watched by the tool) and by the default test run, 49 of 49 files. No brief has been run through it with real sessions. Not built from the user's plan (~/docs/01-feature-stream-plumbing-plan.md): the result collector in a workspace of its own, the submitted, released and accepted boundary, a submission boundary in feature-loop.sh, routing inside wait, early merge and a headless watcher. The work is in the jj workspace run-brief, beside the default line, which a proof run is using.
